conclusion.label: rejects

report:
### Conclusion
While earlier meta-analyses suggested that probiotics might shorten acute diarrhea duration by approximately one day, **current high-quality evidence indicates that probiotics do not effectively treat or shorten acute infectious diarrhea**. Recent clinical trials and updated guidelines advise against relying on them for this purpose.

### Evidence Summary
* **Updated Systematic Reviews:** An updated Cochrane review concluded there is no strong evidence that probiotics are effective for treating acute infectious diarrhea, reversing earlier recommendations after analyzing more rigorous data (https://www.news-medical.net/news/20201209/Researchers-examine-effectiveness-of-treating-acute-infectious-diarrhea-with-probiotics.aspx).
* **Large Clinical Trials:** Multi-center randomized trials evaluating popular formulations (such as *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* GG and combination strains) in emergency department pediatric patients with acute gastroenteritis showed no significant reduction in disease severity or duration compared to placebo (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597, https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/probiotics-not-helpful-young-children-diarrhea).
* **Clinical Guidelines:** The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) clinical practice guidelines recommend against using probiotics in children presenting with acute infectious gastroenteritis due to the lack of clear efficacy across high-quality studies (https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(20)34729-6/fulltext).
